summary: Neo EQ in Graphic mode: Hyperion's 30 bands (bells that overlap and add, as wide as its Bandwidth) summed into its curve, and the curve read at the 31 ISO centres onto the G sliders, which graphic mode's response passes through. Input gain, and whatever the sliders can't reach, go to Output; Highpass into the lowest sliders; Enable to the bypass.

rules.why: Measured on Windows on noise (ReBuzzTests HyperionCalibration, package run 41783615135): each band is the Audio EQ Cookbook's peaking filter at 44.1 kHz, centred on 20 · 1000^(i/29) Hz (its name is rounded), its gain (raw − 128) × 0.1417 dB, its bandwidth warped by ω0/sin ω0 and its alpha at most 1.5 (only the 20 kHz band reaches it); the bands add in dB. That model is within 0.3 dB of every measurement from 40 Hz up (one band at each Bandwidth step, gains ±12 and +18 dB, two neighbours, every band at once at three widths, two zigzags, the top and bottom bands); below 40 Hz within 1.1 dB, where the measurement's 2.7 Hz resolution blurs narrow bands. The curve is read at the exact ISO centres, 1000 · 10^(k/10) Hz.
Enable OFF bypasses Hyperion; Neo EQ has no bypass parameter: the machine's bypass takes it.

remarks: Hyperion's 30 centres step by 0.344 octave, the ISO ones by a third: each Hyperion band lies within 0.17 octave of an ISO centre, and 630 Hz has none of its own. Reading the summed curve at the ISO centres, rather than each slider onto its nearest, costs nothing where the curve is smooth: at the default Bandwidth (2.0 octaves between half-gain points) the model puts every third octave within 0.1 dB; one band at +12 dB at Bandwidth step 2 (0.66 octave) within 0.7 dB and at the narrowest (0.37 octave, step 0) within 1.8 dB, a peak narrower than the sliders' spacing that graphic mode's 2/3-octave bells can't make (its sliders read 7.3 dB at 1 kHz where Hyperion peaks at 12 dB at 904 Hz). Nearest centre instead would miss by 6 to 10 dB for one band and by up to 37 dB for every band at once (Hyperion's overlap).

Hyperion's bands don't compensate their overlap: at the default Bandwidth every band at +6 dB is +43 dB at 3.2 kHz (measured). Where the curve leaves the sliders' ±18 dB it moves as a whole and Output takes the move (beyond ±24 dB, the output connections); a curve spanning more than 36 dB keeps its middle and its ends are clamped, with a note.

Bandwidth is the octaves between a band's half-gain points at low frequencies, twice the number Hyperion displays (1.0 at its default is 2.0 octaves). Highpass is a second-order Butterworth high-pass (Q 0.705 measured) whose corner is 1.28 times the number displayed (28.8 Hz at 22 Hz, 127 Hz at 100 Hz); raw 0, the default, is off. It goes into the sliders after the bands' curve has been placed, so it never moves Output; below its corner graphic mode's cut stops at −18 dB, and below 20 Hz graphic mode settles at the sliders' median instead of cutting.
Hyperion's response is its biquads' at 44.1 kHz; at other rates its high bands move (the cookbook's warping) while graphic mode's don't: the mapping reads Hyperion at 44.1 kHz.
Hyperion is stereo and passes its input at 0 dB at its defaults (measured: right equals left, flat within 0.01 dB).
evidence: ReBuzzTests/AgentReplaceTests.cs HyperionCalibration (Windows, package run 41783615135): its transfer on noise at 6 points an octave (ReBuzzTests/FineTransfer.cs) at its defaults, one band at every Bandwidth step and at −12, +6, +12, +18 dB, two neighbours, the 6.1 and 20 kHz and 20 Hz bands, every band at ±6 dB at four widths, two zigzags, Highpass raw 64 and 127, Input gain raw 60
